newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Kabila expected in S.Africa, timing uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Kabila expected in S.Africa, timing uncertain.

text.p: South Africa said on Tuesday it expected a visit from rebel leader Laurent Kabila to discuss a possible ceasefire in Zaire's civil war but was unsure of the timing of his visit.

Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told parliament's defence committee South Africa would accelerate its efforts to promote peace talks between Kabila's rebel alliance and Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"It is probable Mr Kabila, at the appropriate time, will visit South Africa to get our assessment of how this process has unfolded and what is the way forward," he said.

Pahad, who helped to organise the first direct talks between the Zairean government and rebels earlier this month, said reports that Kabila was in South Africa or expected in the country on Tuesday were premature.

"We, up to date, have not had any formal, official indication that Kabila will be coming into South Africa. He is not in South Africa at the moment. We are still waiting to officially hear when he is arriving, if he is arriving," Pahad said.
He told the committee that Zaire could be on the brink of formal negotiations about a transition to democracy, but said it would be up to Zaireans themselves to settle the details.

"What has happened in an interesting way in the last few days is that both parties have signalled their commitment to meet directly at the principal level in order to negotiate the future dispensation in Zaire," he said.
"For the first time...there is an opportunity for Zaire to achieve the democracy that has eluded it for so long."
Pahad said President Nelson Mandela had discussed the future of Zaire with other African leaders during a brief visit to Angola last week and remained in constant touch with them.

"The three sides, the non-violent opposition as well, believe that ultimately you have to find the possibilities for genuine negotiation which can then lead into a transitional authority, which can then lead to a future democratic dispensation in Zaire," he said.
Pahad said South Africa expected significant and not merely token change in Zaire, but had not taken a position on whether Mobutu should step down after 32 years in power.
"We have had no indication from him that he is willing to go," he said.
Pahad said Mobutu had not requested political asylum in South Africa, but added that such a request would receive "positive" consideration if it were made.
